body.objective: Students will be able to read dotted rhythms.
successCriteria: I can count and perform dotted rhythms
I can explain what a dot does to a note
I can recognize dotted rhythms in songs
body.hook: Have you ever noticed that some songs make you want to move more than others? Often it's because of rhythms that don't land right on the beat. A dot after a note, or an accent in an unexpected place, can turn a plain rhythm into something with groove.

vocabulary.definition: A symbol after a note that adds half the note's value.
A note worth 3 beats in 4/4 time.
A note worth 1½ beats in 4/4 time, often followed by an eighth note.
A curved line joining two notes of the same pitch so they are held as one.
Counting smaller parts of the beat, such as "1-and-2-and."
The feel of a rhythm that makes people want to move.

study.title: Connect the Dots
study.question: How does a dot change rhythm?
study.passage:
The dot rule: a dot adds half the value of the note.
• Half note (2) + dot (1) = dotted half note = 3 beats
• Quarter note (1) + dot (½) = dotted quarter note = 1½ beats
A dotted quarter note is usually followed by an eighth note so the pair fills 2 beats: count "1 (2) and."
Part 1, Subdivide (5 minutes): Count "1-and-2-and-3-and-4-and" aloud while tapping the beat.
Part 2, Tie to dot (10 minutes): Clap a quarter note tied to an eighth note, then see that it sounds exactly like a dotted quarter. Write both versions on the board.
Part 3, Rhythm reading (10 minutes), all in 4/4:
Line 1: dotted half, quarter
Line 2: dotted quarter, eighth, half
Line 3: quarter, dotted quarter, eighth, quarter
Line 4: dotted quarter, eighth, dotted quarter, eighth
Part 4, Listen (5 minutes): Many familiar tunes use a dotted quarter and eighth near the start. Sing or play "Auld Lang Syne" (public domain): the words "auld ac-" (in "auld acquaintance") use a dotted quarter and an eighth.
Part 5, Perform (10 minutes): In groups, perform Lines 1–4 as a round on hand drums or body percussion, keeping a steady beat with a metronome at 80 beats per minute.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; "Auld Lang Syne" is a traditional song in the public domain.
